Q51501.title: Maxwell's equations
paras: Maxwell's equations are the set of equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields are produced by charges and currents and how they change and generate each other. They are named after the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell, who worked them out between 1855 and 1873, building on Michael Faraday's experimental discovery of electromagnetic induction in 1831 and his idea of 'lines of force'.

Maxwell's first paper on the subject, 'On Faraday's Lines of Force', was read to the Cambridge Philosophical Society in 1855 and 1856. In 1861–1862, while professor at King's College London, he published a series of papers, 'On Physical Lines of Force', in which he modelled the field with a mechanical picture of vortices in a medium. His key addition was a new term, the 'displacement current', in Ampère's law. With it the equations predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields, and Maxwell, comparing the calculated speed of these waves with measurements made in 1855 by Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch, found that it was close to the speed of light. He concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

In 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field', presented to the Royal Society in December 1864 and published in 1865, Maxwell derived the electromagnetic wave equation without his mechanical model, and in 1873 he gathered the theory in 'A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism'. His original formulation ran to some twenty equations in components; in the 1880s Oliver Heaviside, alongside work by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Heinrich Hertz, recast them with vector notation into the four equations used today.

Between 1886 and 1889 Hertz produced and detected electromagnetic (radio) waves in the laboratory, confirming Maxwell's prediction. The equations unified electricity, magnetism and optics and became the mathematical basis of electrical, optical and radio technology, from electric motors and power generation to wireless communication and radar. Since the mid-20th century they have been understood as the classical limit of quantum electrodynamics.

Q33132.title: Battle of Gettysburg
paras: The Battle of Gettysburg (1–3 July 1863) was fought in the American Civil War between the Union Army of the Potomac under Major General George G. Meade and the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia under General Robert E. Lee. Some 94,000 Union and 72,000 Confederate soldiers were engaged, by the American Battlefield Trust's count. After his victory at Chancellorsville in May, Lee had marched north in June through the Shenandoah Valley into Pennsylvania, his second invasion of the North, hoping a victory on Union soil would push Northern politicians towards ending the war. Lincoln replaced the hesitant Joseph Hooker with Meade three days before the battle.

On 1 July a Confederate division approaching Gettysburg met Union cavalry under John Buford west of the town. Union infantry came up, and their commander John F. Reynolds was killed; then larger Confederate forces attacking from the northwest and north broke the Union lines, which fell back through the streets to the hills south of the town. On 2 July the Union army held a fishhook-shaped line along Cemetery Ridge and the hills at either end. In the afternoon James Longstreet's corps struck the Union left, with savage fighting at Little Round Top, Devil's Den, the Wheatfield and the Peach Orchard, while attacks on Culp's Hill and Cemetery Hill on the Union right also failed to break through.

On 3 July, after renewed fighting on Culp's Hill, Lee sent about 12,000 men in Pickett's Charge across nearly a mile of open ground against the centre of the Union line on Cemetery Ridge. Union artillery and rifle fire cut them down, and the few who reached the ridge were driven back. On 4 July, the day Vicksburg surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant in the west, Lee began his retreat to Virginia.

With between 46,000 and 51,000 men killed, wounded, captured or missing, Gettysburg was the bloodiest battle of the war. Union losses were about 23,000; Confederate estimates run from about 23,000 to 28,000. Lee never again invaded the North, and the battle is widely seen as a turning point of the war. On 19 November 1863 Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery there.

Q12583.title: Spanish–American War
Q12583.place: Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines
paras: The Spanish–American War of 1898 was fought between the United States and Spain. It grew out of the Cuban War of Independence, which Cuban nationalists had begun against Spanish colonial rule in 1895 and which Spain met with harsh repression, including the forced 'reconcentration' of civilians under General Valeriano Weyler. Reports of Spanish brutality, amplified by the sensationalist American press, built public sympathy in the United States for the rebels; Presidents Grover Cleveland and William McKinley at first resisted calls to intervene.

In January 1898 the US Navy sent the armored cruiser USS Maine to Havana to protect American citizens, and on 15 February it was sunk by an explosion whose cause was never clear. On 20 April McKinley signed a joint resolution of Congress demanding that Spain give up Cuba; its Teller Amendment disclaimed any American intention to annex the island. Spain broke off diplomatic relations, the US Navy began blockading Cuba (on 21 April by Wikipedia's account, 22 April by the State Department historian's), and on 25 April Congress declared that a state of war had existed since 21 April.

The first battle came on 1 May, when Commodore George Dewey's Asiatic Squadron destroyed the Spanish squadron in Manila Bay in the Philippines. In Cuba, US Marines landed at Guantánamo Bay on 10 June, and an army under General William Shafter, including Theodore Roosevelt's volunteer cavalry, the 'Rough Riders', landed east of Santiago de Cuba later in June and fought the battles of El Caney and San Juan Hill on 1 July. On 3 July Admiral Pascual Cervera's squadron tried to break out of Santiago harbour and was destroyed, and Santiago surrendered on 17 July. Guam surrendered without resistance in June, and US troops landed on Puerto Rico on 25 July. American combat deaths were low, but disease, above all typhoid, killed far more soldiers than the fighting.

Hostilities were halted by a protocol of peace signed in Washington on 12 August, and the Treaty of Paris was signed on 10 December 1898. Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, which paid $20 million for the Philippines; the State Department historian notes that the US Senate ratified the treaty in February 1899 by a single vote. The United States also annexed Hawaii during the war. Cuba became formally independent in 1902 but in practice a US protectorate, and American rule in the Philippines led to the Philippine–American War from 1899. The war ended almost four centuries of Spanish empire in the Americas and Asia, made the United States a power in the Pacific and the Caribbean, and in Spain prompted the national soul-searching of the 'Generation of '98'.

Q190712.title: First Battle of the Marne
paras: The First Battle of the Marne was fought in September 1914, in the first weeks of the First World War, between the invading German armies and the French armies under Joseph Joffre together with the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) under Sir John French. Germany's plan, a revised form of the Schlieffen Plan, was to sweep through neutral Belgium and northern France, take Paris and destroy the French army within about six weeks, before turning on Russia. After German victories at the Battles of the Frontiers and Mons in August, the French and British fell back in the 'Great Retreat', and by the start of September German cavalry had crossed the Marne about 40 km (25 miles) from Paris.

The German armies were by then exhausted and had outrun their supplies, while Joffre had moved troops from his eastern flank and from the reserves to his left. Alexander von Kluck's German First Army, instead of keeping level with Karl von Bülow's Second Army, turned south-east east of Paris in pursuit of the French Fifth Army, exposing its flank. On 3 September Joseph Gallieni, the military governor of Paris, saw the opening, and on 4 September Joffre ordered a counter-offensive along a front between Paris and Verdun.

From 5 September Michel-Joseph Maunoury's new French Sixth Army attacked Kluck's flank near the Ourcq river. To strengthen it, Gallieni sent reinforcements forward by rail, lorry and some 600 requisitioned Paris taxis. When Kluck turned his army west to meet this threat, a gap opened between the German First and Second Armies (some 20 miles wide by one account, 30 by another), and from 6 September the BEF and the French Fifth Army under Louis Franchet d'Espèrey pushed into it. Threatened with encirclement, the German First and Second Armies were ordered on 9 September to retreat to the Aisne river, where they dug in.

Sources date the battle to 5–12 September (Wikipedia) or 5–9 September (EBSCO's encyclopedia), the later days covering the German withdrawal. Casualties were heavy: Wikipedia cites estimates of about 250,000 French, 12,733 British and 298,000 German casualties. The battle, remembered in France as the 'miracle of the Marne', saved Paris and ended German hopes of defeating France quickly; Moltke, the German chief of staff, was replaced by Erich von Falkenhayn. Both sides then tried to outflank each other to the north in the 'Race to the Sea', and the Western Front settled into four years of trench warfare.

Q156554.title: Battle of Jutland
Q156554.place: North Sea, off Denmark's Jutland peninsula
paras: The Battle of Jutland, fought on 31 May and 1 June 1916 in the North Sea off Denmark's Jutland peninsula, was the largest naval battle of the First World War and its only full-scale clash of battleships. It pitted the British Grand Fleet under Admiral Sir John Jellicoe, with Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty commanding its battlecruisers, against the German High Seas Fleet under Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer, with Vice-Admiral Franz Hipper leading its scouting battlecruisers. The Germans call it the Battle of the Skagerrak.

Outnumbered in dreadnoughts, the Germans hoped to use Hipper's battlecruisers as bait to draw part of the British fleet onto the guns of their main fleet and destroy it, weakening the British blockade of Germany. But the Admiralty's code-breaking and signals intelligence unit, Room 40, warned of a major sortie, and on the night of 30 May Jellicoe sailed from Scapa Flow to join Beatty before the Germans put to sea.

On the afternoon of 31 May Beatty met Hipper and followed him south towards the High Seas Fleet. In this first phase the British battlecruisers Indefatigable and Queen Mary blew up when their magazines exploded, with almost all their crews. When Beatty sighted the main German fleet he turned north and in turn drew it towards Jellicoe's battleships. In the evening the two full fleets, about 250 ships in all, clashed twice; Jellicoe twice placed his line across the German line of advance, and twice Scheer turned away. The battlecruiser Invincible was sunk in the same phase, and Hipper's flagship Lützow was crippled and later scuttled. During the night Scheer slipped through the light forces behind the Grand Fleet and reached home, losing the old battleship Pommern to a torpedo attack before dawn.

Both sides claimed victory. Fourteen British and eleven German ships were sunk. Wikipedia gives 9,823 casualties in all; by EBSCO's figures more than 6,200 British sailors were killed or captured and about 2,500 Germans killed, so the British lost more ships and more than twice as many men. Yet the British fleet still controlled the North Sea and kept up its blockade. The High Seas Fleet never again sought a fleet battle, and Germany turned instead to its U-boats; its return to unrestricted submarine warfare in early 1917 helped bring the United States into the war that April. The conduct of the battle by Jellicoe and Beatty was argued over in Britain for decades.

Q94916.title: Second Italo-Ethiopian War
paras: The Second Italo-Ethiopian War was a war of conquest waged by Fascist Italy under Benito Mussolini against the Ethiopian Empire of Emperor Haile Selassie, from October 1935 to May 1936. Both countries were members of the League of Nations. Mussolini presented the war as revenge for Italy's defeat by Emperor Menelik II at Adwa in 1896. The pretext was the Walwal incident: Italy had built a fort at the Walwal wells in the Ogaden, well inside Ethiopian territory, and on 5 December 1934 Ethiopian and Italian-led troops there exchanged fire.

On 3 October 1935 Italian forces under Marshal Emilio De Bono crossed the Mareb river from Eritrea without a declaration of war, while a smaller army under General Rodolfo Graziani attacked from Italian Somaliland. Adwa was taken on 6 October. Mussolini, impatient with De Bono's slow progress, replaced him in November with Pietro Badoglio. After an Ethiopian counter-offensive in December, Italy used mustard gas from the air against soldiers and civilians, in breach of the 1925 Geneva Protocol that banned it. From February 1936 the Italians defeated the main Ethiopian armies at Amba Aradam, Tembien and Shire, and the emperor's own army at Maychew on 31 March.

Haile Selassie left the country on 2 May, Badoglio's forces entered Addis Ababa on 5 May, and on 9 May Mussolini proclaimed the annexation of Ethiopia and the founding of an Italian empire. The League of Nations condemned Italy as the aggressor and voted economic sanctions in October 1935 (taking effect in November), but they left out oil, coal and iron or steel, and Britain did not close the Suez Canal to Italian shipping. The League voted on 4 July 1936 to end them, and they were formally withdrawn on 15 July. A British–French compromise, the Hoare–Laval plan, collapsed when it leaked in December 1935.

The war killed hundreds of thousands of Ethiopians, many of them civilians, and guerrilla resistance to Italian rule continued until Ethiopia was liberated in 1941. Its diplomatic effects reached far beyond Africa: the League's failure to stop the invasion discredited it, and Italy drifted away from Britain and France towards Nazi Germany. Many historians see the crisis as one of the steps towards the Second World War.

Q127050.title: Manhattan Project
Q127050.place: United States (Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Hanford and other sites)
paras: The Manhattan Project was the Second World War programme that built the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States with the United Kingdom and Canada, and absorbed Britain's own bomb project, Tube Alloys. Its roots lay in the discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Germany in 1938. In August 1939 Leo Szilard and Eugene Wigner drafted a letter, signed by Albert Einstein, warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt that a new kind of extremely powerful bomb might be possible; Roosevelt set up an Advisory Committee on Uranium, and early research went slowly until Britain's MAUD Committee reported in 1941 that a bomb was feasible.

In 1942 the US Army Corps of Engineers took over the work. The Manhattan District, named after its first headquarters in New York, was created on 13 August 1942, and from September General Leslie Groves directed the whole project; the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer led the weapons laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico. On 2 December 1942 a team under Enrico Fermi achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1. Most of the money went on making fissile material: uranium was enriched at Oak Ridge (the Clinton Engineer Works) in Tennessee, and plutonium was made in the first industrial-scale reactors at Hanford in Washington State. At its peak the project employed nearly 130,000 people, and it cost nearly $2 billion.

Los Alamos produced two designs: Little Boy, a gun-type bomb using enriched uranium, and Fat Man, a more complex implosion bomb using plutonium. The first nuclear explosion, of an implosion device, was the Trinity test in the New Mexico desert on 16 July 1945. On 6 August 1945 Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima, and on 9 August Fat Man on Nagasaki; Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. After the war the project kept control of American nuclear research and production until the civilian Atomic Energy Commission took over in January 1947.

Q80130.title: Nuremberg trials
paras: The Nuremberg trials were the trials of the surviving leaders of Nazi Germany held after the Second World War by the four main Allied powers: the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France. During the war the Allies had argued over what to do with the Nazi leaders, with proposals ranging from summary execution to a show trial. In the London (Nuremberg) Charter of 8 August 1945 they agreed on an International Military Tribunal and defined the crimes it would try: crimes against peace (planning and waging wars of aggression), war crimes, and crimes against humanity. The trial was held in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, which had survived the bombing and had a prison attached.

The main trial before the tribunal ran from 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946. Hitler, Himmler and Goebbels were already dead by suicide. Of the 24 men indicted, 22 were tried, including Hermann Göring, Joachim von Ribbentrop, the military chiefs Wilhelm Keitel and Alfred Jodl, Rudolf Hess and Albert Speer; Martin Bormann was tried in absentia, since the Allies did not know he was dead. Six Nazi organisations were also charged. The US chief prosecutor was Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, who wanted the trial also to put an irrefutable record of Nazi crimes before the world; the Holocaust was a major focus of the evidence. The main defence argument was that the charges, especially that of aggressive war, were new law applied retroactively.

The tribunal convicted 19 defendants and acquitted three: Franz von Papen, Hjalmar Schacht and Hans Fritzsche. Twelve, including Bormann in absentia, were sentenced to death and the rest to prison terms from ten years to life. Ten were hanged on 16 October 1946; Göring killed himself the night before. Four organisations were declared criminal: the Nazi Party's Leadership Corps, the SS, the Gestapo and the SD.

Between 1946 and 1949 the United States held twelve further trials at Nuremberg of lower-ranking defendants such as doctors, judges and industrialists, which concentrated more on the Holocaust. Though criticised at the time as victors' justice and for punishing acts that had not been crimes when committed, the trials established that individuals can be held criminally responsible for breaking international law, and they are regarded as the start of modern international criminal law.

Q171375.title: Truman Doctrine
paras: The Truman Doctrine was the American foreign policy announced by President Harry S. Truman in a speech to a joint session of Congress on 12 March 1947, pledging US support to countries threatened by communist takeover from within or by Soviet pressure from outside. Its immediate occasions were Greece and Turkey. In Greece the government was fighting a civil war against Communist guerrillas, who were helped by Tito's Yugoslavia; in Turkey the Soviet Union was pressing for base and transit rights in the Turkish Straits. Britain, which had been supporting both countries, told Washington early in 1947 that because of its own economic troubles it would end its aid to Greece (from 31 March, according to the State Department historian).

By then relations between the wartime allies had soured over Soviet troops lingering in northern Iran, the Straits, and the Soviet rejection of the Baruch plan for international control of atomic energy, and George Kennan's 'Long Telegram' of February 1946 had argued for containing Soviet expansion. Washington believed, wrongly, that Moscow was behind the Greek Communists; in fact Stalin had held back from helping them. Truman, encouraged by the Republican Senator Arthur Vandenberg to make the threat plain to the American public, asked Congress for $400 million in aid to Greece and Turkey, together with American civilian and military personnel.

Truman declared that 'it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures', arguing that the spread of totalitarian rule threatened international peace and American security, and that if Greece fell, Turkey and the Middle East would be endangered. In May 1947 Congress approved the $400 million by a large majority.

The doctrine broke with the American tradition of avoiding peacetime commitments outside the Western Hemisphere and became the basis of US containment policy in the Cold War; historians often date the start of the Cold War from Truman's speech. It was followed by the Marshall Plan for Western Europe's economic recovery and by the creation of NATO in 1949.

Q151349.title: Berlin Blockade
paras: After the Second World War, defeated Germany and its capital Berlin were each divided into American, British, French and Soviet zones of occupation. Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, and the Western sectors of the city depended on road, rail and canal links across it. By 1948 the wartime allies had fallen out over Germany's future. The United States and Britain had merged their zones into 'Bizonia' in 1947, the Marshall Plan was beginning, and in early 1948 the three Western powers began planning a West German state; in March the Soviets walked out of the Allied Control Council that coordinated the occupation. In June the Western powers introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, in their zones and in West Berlin.

The Soviet Union replied with its own currency and, on 24 June 1948, cut all road, rail and canal access to West Berlin, cutting West Berlin off from its regular supplies of food, coal and electricity; it offered to lift the blockade if the Deutsche Mark was withdrawn from West Berlin. The American military governor, General Lucius Clay, argued that staying in Berlin had become a symbol of American resolve. Because a 1945 agreement guaranteed the Western Allies three air corridors into the city, the United States began an airlift, 'Operation Vittles', on 26 June, and Britain joined two days later with 'Operation Plainfare'. Crews from Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa flew with the RAF.

The airlift became steadily larger and more efficient. By the time it officially ended on 30 September 1949 it had flown in about 2.3 million tons of supplies, nearly two-thirds of it coal, on more than 270,000 flights. Seventeen American and eight British aircraft crashed during the operation. In September 1948 some 300,000 West Berliners rallied at the Reichstag against Soviet domination. Facing an Allied counter-blockade of its own zone and seeing that the airlift could be kept up indefinitely, Moscow lifted the blockade in May 1949 (on 12 May by most accounts; the State Department historian's page gives both 11 and 12 May).

The crisis hardened the division of Germany and Europe. Shortly before the blockade ended, the Western Allies created the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO); about two weeks after it ended the West German state, the Federal Republic of Germany, was established, soon followed by East Germany. West Berlin, once identified with Prussian militarism and Nazism, became a symbol of Western freedom in the Cold War.

Q877399.title: North Atlantic Treaty
paras: The North Atlantic Treaty, also called the Washington Treaty, was signed in Washington, D.C., on 4 April 1949 by twelve countries: the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, Italy and Portugal. It created the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), a collective-defence alliance against the Soviet Union, and was the first peacetime military alliance the United States had entered outside the Western Hemisphere.

Western European governments had grown alarmed in 1947–1948: by the civil war in Greece and pressure on Turkey, the Communist coup in Czechoslovakia in 1948, Communist strength in the Italian elections, and the Soviet blockade of West Berlin from June 1948. In March 1948 Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the Brussels Treaty, a mutual-defence pact, and secret talks at the Pentagon that spring agreed in principle on a wider treaty. In May 1948 Senator Arthur Vandenberg proposed a resolution, which the Senate passed, backing a security treaty with Western Europe within the UN Charter but outside the Security Council, where the Soviets had a veto. Negotiations followed over how firm an American commitment could be, given that only Congress can declare war, and over whether to bring in North Atlantic countries beyond the Brussels powers.

The core of the treaty is Article 5: an armed attack on one member in Europe or North America is to be treated as an attack on all, and each will take 'such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force' to restore security. Article 6 limited this to members' territory in Europe and North America and certain North Atlantic areas, excluding colonial territories elsewhere.

Later in 1949 the US Congress passed the Mutual Defense Assistance Program to help rearm Western Europe, and after the Korean War began in 1950 the allies built an integrated military command. Greece and Turkey joined in 1952 and West Germany in 1955, after which the Soviet Union formed the Warsaw Pact. Article 5 was never invoked during the Cold War; its only invocation came after the September 11 attacks on the United States in 2001. By 2025 the treaty had 32 member states.

Q11264.title: Cuban Revolution
paras: The Cuban Revolution was the armed movement that overthrew Fulgencio Batista, who had seized power in Cuba in a military coup in March 1952, ending the country's constitutional government. Among the coup's opponents was Fidel Castro, a young lawyer, who first challenged it in the courts. When that failed, he and his brother Raúl led an attack on the Moncada army barracks in Santiago de Cuba on 26 July 1953. The attack failed, many of the attackers were killed, and Castro was captured and imprisoned; his speech at the trial made him famous across Cuba, and the date gave its name to his 26th of July Movement.

Batista, seeking public approval, later amnestied the surviving attackers, and the Castros went into exile in Mexico, where they met the Argentine revolutionary Ernesto 'Che' Guevara. In late 1956 Castro and a small band of fighters sailed back to Cuba's eastern coast in the yacht Granma. Government troops attacked them on landing, and a small group of survivors, among them Fidel and Raúl Castro and Guevara, escaped into the Sierra Maestra mountains. From there the guerrillas grew into an army, while urban resistance groups such as the Revolutionary Directorate fought Batista in the cities.

Batista's support ebbed. In March 1958 the United States, which had been supplying his forces, imposed an arms embargo on his government. That summer a large army offensive into the mountains, Operation Verano, failed. The rebels then went on the attack, and on 31 December 1958 columns under Guevara and Camilo Cienfuegos, together with Revolutionary Directorate fighters, took the city of Santa Clara. Batista fled to the Dominican Republic in the early hours of 1 January 1959, and rebel forces entered Havana; Castro arrived there on 8 January.

Manuel Urrutia became president and Castro soon became prime minister, quickly concentrating power in his own hands. Revolutionary tribunals tried and executed members of the old regime. Castro's government moved towards the Soviet Union and Marxism–Leninism: the 26th of July Movement was later merged into the Communist Party of Cuba, founded in 1965, and Cuba became the first communist state in the Western Hemisphere. Relations with the United States broke down, leading to an American trade embargo, the failed CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Q604897.title: Battle of Dien Bien Phu
paras: The Battle of Điện Biên Phủ (13 March – 7 May 1954) was the decisive battle of the First Indochina War, fought between the forces of the French Union and the Communist-led Viet Minh independence movement of Ho Chi Minh, whose army was commanded by General Võ Nguyên Giáp. Since 1946 France had been fighting to keep control of Vietnam, with growing financial help from the United States, which saw the war as part of the struggle against Communist expansion in Asia.

In 1953 the French commander, General Henri Navarre, decided to plant a heavily fortified base, supplied by air, in a remote valley at Điện Biên Phủ near the Laotian border, to block Viet Minh routes into Laos and to draw Giáp into a pitched battle where French firepower could destroy his army. French paratroopers seized the valley on 20 November 1953, and the garrison eventually reached nearly 16,000 men. The French assumed the Viet Minh could not bring heavy guns, especially anti-aircraft guns, through the surrounding mountains. Instead, Giáp's troops dragged artillery up the hills overlooking the valley and dug it into well-hidden emplacements.

On 13 March 1954 the Viet Minh opened a massive bombardment and stormed the strongpoint Béatrice that night; other outlying positions fell in the following days. The French artillery could not silence the hidden guns, and their artillery commander, Colonel Charles Piroth, killed himself. As the airstrip came under fire and aircraft were shot down, the garrison depended on parachute drops, while the perimeter shrank under trench-by-trench fighting. France appealed for American air strikes; President Eisenhower would not intervene without allies, and Britain refused to take part. On 7 May the last positions were overrun and the surviving defenders surrendered, after a siege that Wikipedia counts as two months and the State Department historian as four.

The defeat was a profound shock in France. At the Geneva Conference, which reached agreement ten weeks after the battle, the French agreed to leave Indochina. Vietnam was temporarily divided at the 17th parallel, with Ho Chi Minh's Democratic Republic of Vietnam in the North and the State of Vietnam in the South, with nationwide elections promised for 1956. The United States, which did not sign the final agreement, took France's place as the backer of South Vietnam, a commitment that drew it ever deeper into Vietnam for the next twenty years.

Q389646.title: Baltic Way
paras: The Baltic Way was a peaceful protest on 23 August 1989 in which about two million people joined hands in a human chain running from Vilnius through Riga to Tallinn, across the three Baltic republics then ruled by the Soviet Union. It was organised by the three countries' popular independence movements, Lithuania's Sąjūdis, the Popular Front of Latvia and the Popular Front of Estonia, and it marked the 50th anniversary of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 1939.

That pact between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had contained secret protocols dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence, and in 1940 the Soviet Union occupied and annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Moscow long denied that the secret protocols existed and held that the Baltic states had joined the Soviet Union voluntarily; for the independence movements, proof of the protocols meant that the annexation had been illegal. Tension with Moscow grew through the summer of 1989. The idea of a chain seems to have been put forward at a meeting of the three movements in Pärnu, Estonia, on 15 July. On 18 August Alexander Yakovlev, who headed a Soviet commission on the pact, admitted in Pravda that the secret protocols were genuine.

On the evening of 23 August people stood along the roads between the three capitals and linked hands for 15 minutes at 19:00 local time; buses and radio broadcasts helped fill gaps in the line. The length of the chain is given as about 675 km by Wikipedia and about 650 km by the Baltic military-heritage project's account. It was one of the longest unbroken human chains ever formed, and for a time Guinness listed it as the longest.

The protest put the case for Baltic independence before the world as a moral as well as a political issue. In December 1989 the Soviet Congress of People's Deputies accepted the Yakovlev commission's report condemning the secret protocols. On 11 March 1990 Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence, and all three Baltic states regained their independence in 1991. In 2009 the documents recording the Baltic Way were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, and 23 August is now marked in Europe as a day of remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism.

Q221382.title: 1991 Soviet coup attempt
paras: In August 1991 a group of hard-line Communist officials tried to seize power from the Soviet president, Mikhail Gorbachev. The eight members of their self-styled State Committee on the State of Emergency included Vice President Gennady Yanayev, KGB chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov, Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov, Interior Minister Boris Pugo and Prime Minister Valentin Pavlov, several of them men Gorbachev had appointed himself. They opposed his reforms and, above all, the New Union Treaty, due to be signed on 20 August, which would have shifted much of the central government's power to the fifteen union republics. Their chief opponent turned out to be Boris Yeltsin, the elected president of the Russian republic.

On 18 August a delegation of the plotters visited Gorbachev at his holiday house at Foros in Crimea and demanded that he back a state of emergency; when he refused, he was held there, cut off from the outside world. Early on 19 August the committee announced that Gorbachev was ill, that Yanayev had taken over his powers, and that a state of emergency was in force. Tanks and troops were sent into Moscow. But the plotters failed to arrest Yeltsin. He reached the White House, the Russian parliament building, declared the coup illegal and, climbing onto a tank outside, called on people to resist; the scene was broadcast around the world.

Crowds built barricades around the White House, and some army units went over to Yeltsin. In the early hours of 21 August three young men, Dmitry Komar, Vladimir Usov and Ilya Krichevsky, were killed in a clash with armoured vehicles in a tunnel near the parliament. The troops and elite KGB units would not storm the building, and the coup collapsed later that day. Gorbachev returned to Moscow, Pugo killed himself, and the other leaders were arrested.

The failed coup destroyed what was left of the Soviet system. Gorbachev came back much weakened and Yeltsin far stronger. Gorbachev resigned as head of the Communist Party, which was blamed for the coup; its activities were suspended across the Soviet Union within days, and Russia banned it in November. Within days Ukraine and other republics declared independence. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president, and the next day the Soviet Union was formally dissolved.

Q131297.title: 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi
paras: Between April and July 1994, during the Rwandan Civil War, Hutu extremists in Rwanda's government, army and militias systematically killed members of the Tutsi minority, together with moderate Hutu and some Twa. The roots lay in decades of ethnic division. Under Belgian colonial rule the Tutsi minority had been favoured; the Hutu uprising that began in 1959 ended Tutsi dominance and drove many Tutsi into exile in neighbouring countries before independence in 1962. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), a mainly Tutsi rebel force formed among the refugees, invaded from Uganda. The Arusha peace agreements of August 1993 were meant to end the war, and the UN sent a peacekeeping mission (UNAMIR), but extremists were meanwhile preparing a campaign of extermination, arming militias such as the Interahamwe.

On the evening of 6 April 1994 the aircraft carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana of Rwanda and the president of Burundi was shot down over Kigali. Within hours the Presidential Guard, soldiers and militiamen set up roadblocks to identify Tutsi and began killing them. On 7 April the moderate Hutu prime minister, Agathe Uwilingiyimana, was murdered, along with ten Belgian peacekeepers guarding her, and the extremist radio station RTLM urged listeners to kill the 'cockroaches'. The massacres spread across the country; many victims were killed by neighbours, often with machetes, and sexual violence was widespread.

The world failed to intervene. Belgium withdrew its troops, and on 21 April, by the UN's own account, UNAMIR was cut from 2,165 to 270 soldiers. A French-led operation, Operation Turquoise, entered the south-west in June; it saved some civilians but also let some of the killers escape. The genocide ended only when the RPF defeated the government forces and took control of the country in July.

The death toll is disputed: the UN outreach programme and Rwanda's constitution put it above one million, HISTORY.com at as many as 800,000, and most scholarly estimates between about 500,000 and 662,000 Tutsi. About two million mostly Hutu refugees, among them many of the killers, fled into neighbouring countries, chiefly Zaire, which helped set off the First Congo War in 1996. On 8 November 1994, according to the UN (HISTORY.com says October), the Security Council set up the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in Arusha, Tanzania, which indicted 93 people and sentenced the interim government's prime minister, Jean Kambanda, to life imprisonment.

Q81545.title: Libyan Civil War (2011)
paras: The Libyan Civil War of 2011 was fought between forces loyal to Muammar Gaddafi, who had ruled Libya for 42 years, and rebels seeking to overthrow him. Inspired by the Arab Spring, protests began in Benghazi on 15 February 2011, triggered by the arrest of government critics, including a lawyer for the families of prisoners killed in Tripoli's Abu Salim prison in 1996. Opponents called 17 February a 'day of revolt'. Security forces fired on the crowds, and the protests turned into an armed rebellion; by about 20 February the rebels held Benghazi, and much of eastern Libya and several western towns soon slipped from Gaddafi's control. The rebels formed an interim body, the National Transitional Council (NTC).

On 26 February the UN Security Council passed Resolution 1970, imposing an arms embargo and sanctions on Gaddafi and his circle and referring Libya to the International Criminal Court. In early March government forces counter-attacked, retook several coastal towns and closed in on Benghazi. On 17 March the Security Council passed Resolution 1973, authorising a no-fly zone and 'all necessary measures', short of an occupation force, to protect civilians; Russia, China, India, Germany and Brazil abstained. Air strikes began on 19 March, with French jets striking first, and the campaign was soon run by NATO, which stopped the assault on Benghazi and increasingly gave air support to the rebels.

Fighting swung back and forth for months; the port city of Misrata endured a siege of about two months before government forces withdrew in May. In August rebel forces advanced along the coast and from the Western Mountains, and on 21 August entered Tripoli; Gaddafi escaped capture. On 16 September the UN recognised the NTC as Libya's representative. On 20 October NTC fighters took Gaddafi's home town of Sirte, and Gaddafi was captured nearby and killed. On 23 October the NTC declared Libya liberated.

The war's toll included abuses on both sides, among them the apparent execution of 53 Gaddafi supporters in Sirte by militiamen from Misrata and the barring of some 30,000 people of the town of Tawergha from returning home, both documented by Human Rights Watch. The NTC struggled to control the many armed militias the war had created and to collect their weapons. These unresolved conflicts led to continuing instability and eventually to a second Libyan civil war.

Q194378.title: Third Servile War
paras: The Third Servile War (73–71 BC), also called the War of Spartacus, was the last and most dangerous of the great slave revolts against the Roman Republic, and the only one fought in Italy itself. Rome's wars of conquest had flooded Italy with slaves, many of them working on large estates. In 73 BC a group of gladiators broke out of the gladiator school of Lentulus Batiatus at Capua; the ancient accounts put them at about 70 (Wikipedia, following Plutarch) or 78 (the Livius account). They chose leaders, the Thracian Spartacus, Crixus and Oenomaus, and took refuge on Mount Vesuvius, while runaway slaves flocked to join them.

Rome at first treated the revolt as banditry. The praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber besieged the rebels on Vesuvius with some 3,000 hastily raised militiamen, but the slaves climbed down the cliffs on ropes made of vines, took his camp by surprise and destroyed his force; a second praetorian army was also beaten. With much of Rome's strength tied up in wars in Spain and against Mithridates in the east, the slave army grew to tens of thousands and plundered southern Italy. In 72 BC the Senate sent both consuls, Lucius Gellius Publicola and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus. Gellius destroyed a separate band under Crixus near Mount Garganus, but Spartacus defeated the consular armies, marched north and beat the governor of Cisalpine Gaul near Mutina (Modena). Instead of crossing the Alps, the rebels turned back south.

The Senate then gave the command to Marcus Licinius Crassus, with eight legions. Crassus restored discipline, reportedly by decimating units that had fled, and pursued Spartacus into Bruttium, the toe of Italy, where the rebels hoped to cross to Sicily with the help of Cilician pirates who never came. Crassus walled them in across the peninsula, but Spartacus broke out. With Pompey's army returning from Spain, Spartacus turned to fight, and in 71 BC his army was destroyed in a final battle in Lucania, by the Silarius river according to Wikipedia. Spartacus was killed, though his body was never found. Pompey's troops cut down some 5,000 fugitives, and about 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way between Capua and Rome.

Crassus and Pompey both used their victories to win the consulship for 70 BC, backed by the presence of their armies, an episode that historians see as a step in the decline of the Republic's institutions. In modern times Spartacus became a symbol of resistance to oppression.

Q131386.title: Battle of Alesia
paras: The siege of Alesia in 52 BC was the decisive battle of Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars. Caesar had been conquering Gaul since 58 BC. In 52 BC many Gallic tribes rose together under a young Arvernian nobleman, Vercingetorix, who tried to starve Caesar's legions by burning towns and supplies and harrying Roman foragers with his cavalry. Caesar took the stronghold of Avaricum (Bourges) but failed to take Gergovia, Vercingetorix's home town; then, after a defeat of the Gallic cavalry, Vercingetorix withdrew with a large army into Alesia, a hilltop town of the Mandubii, usually identified with Mont Auxois above Alise-Sainte-Reine in eastern France.

Rather than assault the strong position, Caesar besieged it. His troops built an inner ring of fortifications facing the town, about 16 km long by Caesar's figures as summarised by Wikipedia (about 15 km by the Livius account), with ditches, walls, towers and fields of hidden stakes and spikes. Knowing that a Gallic relief army was being raised, they then built a second, outer ring of about 21 km facing outwards, so that the Romans were themselves enclosed between two lines. As food in Alesia ran out, Vercingetorix expelled the town's civilians, but the Romans would not let them through their lines, and they were left trapped between the two sides.

The relief army arrived and, together with the defenders, attacked the Roman lines several times over a few days. The heaviest attack fell on a weak spot in the north-west, where a hill could not be included in the works; there a picked force under Vercassivellaunus, a relative of Vercingetorix, nearly broke through. Caesar sent Titus Labienus with reinforcements and then came himself, and the attack was beaten off. The relief army broke up, and the next day Vercingetorix surrendered.

Caesar handed most of the prisoners to his soldiers as slaves, sparing the Aedui and the Arverni to win them back. Vercingetorix was held in Rome for years, paraded in Caesar's triumph in 46 BC and then executed. Mopping-up campaigns continued, but Alesia ended organised Gallic resistance, and Gaul became Roman. The Senate voted Caesar 20 days of thanksgiving but, for political reasons, not a triumph at the time; political tension in Rome grew, and in 49 BC Caesar crossed the Rubicon and began a civil war.

Q369560.title: Siege of Baghdad (1258)
paras: In early 1258 a Mongol army under Hulegu (Hulagu), a grandson of Genghis Khan and brother of the Great Khan Möngke, besieged and sacked Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid Caliphate for five centuries and one of the great centres of learning of the Islamic world. Sent west to secure Persia, Hulegu had destroyed the Nizari Ismaili 'Assassins' and their fortress of Alamut in 1256. He demanded that the caliph al-Musta'sim submit; the caliph refused and boasted that an attack on Baghdad would rouse the whole Muslim world against the Mongols, and Hulegu decided at the end of 1257 to take the city by force.

The Mongol columns converged on Baghdad from several directions. On 17 January 1258 they routed the caliph's field army west of the city after flooding the plain behind it by breaking the dykes, and by 22 January they had surrounded Baghdad on both banks of the Tigris. The assault began on 29 January (some sources say 30 January). Siege engines breached the Ajami tower in the eastern wall, which fell on 1 February, and by 3–4 February the Mongols held the whole eastern wall. The caliph's embassies and offers of tribute were refused. On 10 February 1258 al-Musta'sim came out and surrendered the city.

The Mongols then sacked Baghdad for about a week. Christians, on whose behalf Hulegu's Christian wife Doquz Khatun interceded, and some other groups were spared; most of the rest of the population suffered killing and plunder. The number of dead is unknown: estimates range from nearly 80,000 (in the modern account excerpted by De Re Militari) to the 800,000 to two million of later Muslim writers, and Hulegu himself claimed two million in a letter to Louis IX of France, a figure historians regard as inflated; an epidemic after the sack added to the deaths. After the pillage ended, al-Musta'sim was put to death with his family, according to the usual account wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses, since the Mongols avoided shedding royal blood (another account says he was strangled).

The fall of Baghdad ended the Abbasid Caliphate there after some 500 years; a member of the dynasty was later installed as caliph in Cairo by the Mamluks, but only as a figurehead. The sack has traditionally been seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age, although historians now debate its long-term effects, and Baghdad recovered under Hulegu's Ilkhanate, though it was overshadowed by the new capital, Tabriz.
